newsitem.title: USA: Weather saps building at close of strong 1996.
newsitem.headline: Weather saps building at close of strong 1996.

text.p: Bitter weather on the West Coast sapped new-home building in December, the government said on Wednesday, bringing the industry's best year since 1988 to a weak close.

Starts on new homes and apartment buildings tumbled 12.2 percent from November's pace to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.33 million last month, the Commerce Department said. It was the weakest rate in 1-1/2 years, since 1.3 million in June 1995.
Analysts said home building would probably slow in 1997, though not precipitously, as job growth and income gains also slow after a vigorous 1996 and mortgage rates edge up.
For all of 1996, builders broke ground on 1.47 million new homes, up 8.9 percent from 1.35 million in 1995. It was the highest since 1.49 million homes were started in 1988.
Separately, the Federal Reserve issued its Beige Book report on the national economy showing steady, moderate expansion early in 1997 with little upward pressure on prices.

"Economic growth in December and early January was moderate in most parts of the country," the central bank said, based on interviews conducted with business owners in all 12 districts where regional Fed banks are based.
It buttressed analysts' expectations that Fed policy-makers, who will use the report when they meet on Feb. 4-5 to plot interest rate strategy, will leave rates unchanged.
The Fed noted "scattered evidence of increasing wage pressures" but did sound an alarming tone on inflation.

Weaker December housing starts were expected to slow the rate of increase in fourth-quarter gross domestic product because residential construction is a significant contributor to the economy, further reducing pressure on the Fed to act to curb activity.

"Both the interest-rate swing and the slowdown in job growth inevitably was going to take some steam out of the housing market and it clearly has happened," said economist David Seiders of the National Association of Home Builders.

Seiders said 1997 starts would probably fall 6 percent or so from last year to about 1.38 million units, which he said was still a healthy rate, especially since there has been scant sign of excess inventories of completed, unsold homes.
While mortgage rates edged lower last month, they remained well above their levels a year earlier.
Every region reported a lower rate of starts in December, but the biggest drop came in the West, where starts plunged 29.2 percent to an annual rate of 257,000.
That was the lowest rate in the region, which includes the big California market as well as Washington and Oregon, since February 1993, when the rate also was 257,000.
The West was pummeled by heavy snows, flooding and mudslides in December, which analysts said had an impact on the monthly figures despite efforts to adjust them for seasonal influences.
"When you have floods, you can't see holes in the ground," said economist David Lereah of the Mortgage Bankers Association. He said starts will likely slow to around 1.35 million units this year.
"It's clear the housing sector is coming off its highs from late summer," Lereah said. "It's going to be at a healthy pace in 1997 but off its peaks."
All regions reported weaker December building. In the Northeast, starts fell 2.3 percent from November to 125,000 a year and in the Midwest they fell 7.9 percent to 302,000.
Construction starts in the South, the biggest regional market, dropped 7.2 percent to an annual rate of 645,000.

Analysts and builders expect the market to steady in January, since the drop in applications for building permits was a scant 0.6 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.41 million. That followed a 4.1 percent November gain.
The National Association of Home Builders said last week that its index of market activity was down moderately in January but said the market appeared to be steadying.
Mortgage rates have moved higher in recent weeks, a potential dampening influence.

The Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp., or Freddie Mac, said rates for a 30-year loan averaged 7.60 percent in December, down from 7.62 percent in November, but higher than December 1995's 7.17 percent.
